_: One paragraph per neighbourhood, written by us from the Board's records.
_how: Each paragraph is read out of the neighbourhood's own records — the file `website/public/data/us/sf/city/blocks/hood/<i>.json` plus the shards behind it. Every clause carries a record in `sources`, so a reader can check any sentence against the page it came from and an editor can see what a sentence is standing on. Nothing is written that no record supports.
_voice: Say what happened. Do not characterise motive, tone or reason unless the record states it. No adjectives the record does not earn. If the neighbourhood's records do not add up to something worth a paragraph, leave it out — a missing summary is honest, a padded one is not.
_read: `read.full` is the year range read line by line; `read.sampled` is what was only sampled. A paragraph may not claim anything about a period that was only sampled.
_partial: THIS FILE IS PARTIAL AND SAYS SO. Neighbourhoods absent from `hoods` have no paragraph and their page opens on the record, which is the correct behaviour and not a bug.

0.name: Bayview Hunters Point
0.summary: For thirty years after 1906 the Board was mostly grading and paving this district into existence, avenue by avenue, and granting railways the spur tracks to run into its plants. It holds the city's sewage plant, its wholesale produce market and its wrecking yards, and in 2000 the Board asked the state to put a parole office somewhere else. Its Opera House has stood on Third Street since at least 1924, and the city was still protecting it in 2010. Streets were closed for the Girls' Club festival in 1973 and for the opening of the Senior Center in 1981, and in the late 1990s the Board of Supervisors came out and held its own meetings here.

12.name: Japantown
12.summary: In 1910 neighbours petitioned the Board against a laundry a man named Mori wanted to open on Sutter Street. In the 1950s and 60s the city widened Geary and Webster through here — its own engineers called Webster the first stage of a thoroughfare running through the heart of the Western Addition redevelopment area. Buchanan Street was closed to traffic in 1974, and the neighbourhood has been closing Post Street for the Obon dance and the Nihonmachi Street Fair almost every summer since. In 1997, and again in 2001, the Board took the side of the Soko Bukai in its claim on the YWCA building at 1830 Sutter Street.

3.name: Chinatown
3.summary: In 1912 the city paid $24,000 for land at 929 Clay Street and built the Oriental School on it — the segregated school for Chinese children — repairing its roof in 1919 and adding an annex in 1923. In 1913 it ordered the Stockton Street tunnel dug under the hill, having thrown out one assessment report and set a date to hear the protests over who would pay. The neighbourhood closes its own streets more than almost any other: Joice Street for a youth carnival in 1970, and Filbert Street every weekday at 11:40 through the winter of 1978 so that schoolchildren had somewhere to spend their lunch break. In 1996 the Board urged the YWCA to give the Chinese community time to bid for its building at 965 Clay Street, and then lent the Chinese Historical Society the money to buy it.

40.name: Western Addition
40.summary: In 1930 the Booker T. Washington Community Center held a masquerade ball at the Scottish Rite Hall. From 1953 the city widened Geary and Webster through the district — its own engineers wrote that Webster was the first stage of a thoroughfare traversing the heart of the Western Addition redevelopment area — and went on vacating streets inside that project area for twenty years after: O'Farrell in 1961, Buchanan and Birch in 1974, O'Farrell and Ellis again in 1981. Through the 1980s the district filled with condominium projects, one of them 247 units on its own. Since 1978 it has closed Divisadero, and then Fillmore, every June for Juneteenth.

22.name: North Beach
22.summary: This neighbourhood shuts its own streets more than most: for Columbus Day at Sts Peter and Paul, for the annual Blessing of the Fishing Fleet, for the Upper Grant Avenue Street Fair — already in its twenty-ninth year by 1982 — and once for Coit Tower's fiftieth birthday. 8.name: Haight Ashbury
8.summary: The Haight has closed its own street for a fair since the 1970s — the ninth was in 1986 — and closed Cole Street for political rallies since at least 1980. In 1996 the Board put interim controls on Haight Street to stop new places selling alcohol from opening. In 2005 it asked the city to look into residents repeatedly finding syringes on Cole Street, and in the same year commended the 409 House on Clayton Street for its contributions to community activism. Two of the neighbourhood's trees are landmarks in their own right: a black acacia on Masonic Avenue and a coast redwood at 313 Scott Street.

35.name: Tenderloin
35.summary: For the last several years this neighbourhood's record has been the city taking over its hotels. It leased the Adante on Geary Street and the Monarch further up the same street as temporary shelter, extended its lease on the Pacific Bay Inn on Jones, and kept 459 rooms at 1231 Market. In 2019 it let 101 Hyde Street, a building it owns, to La Cocina for $12,000 a year, with a million-dollar gift from the San Francisco Foundation behind it. Liquor licences move from address to address here more than anywhere else in the city.

2.name: Castro/Upper Market
2.summary: This is a hill, and for its first thirty years the record is the city trying to get streets onto it. The Board kept re-setting the official grades on Saturn, Temple and Lower Terrace, licensed contractors to set off blasts on Upper Terrace, and where a roadway would not go it ordered a stairway instead — one from the low level of Ord Street up to Market in 1931. The flat ground at the bottom held the horses: 184 of them at the United Milk Company's stable on Sixteenth Street in 1915, sixty more behind 125-135 Landers Street the year before. Until about 1930 the Board also voted on every fuel-oil tank and boiler, so the record names the shops one at a time — the Original Fairville Creamery heating water for its dairy at 444 Castro Street, Hugo's Pastry Shop at 524, the Eureka Valley Bakery over on Eighteenth. Two schools went up and their land was bought a parcel at a time, Mission High on Dolores Street and Everett on Sanchez, where the Board was still paying out of the school tax for one lot after another in 1923. The Twin Peaks Tunnel was driven under the ridge, and by 1914 the City Attorney was advising on how to avoid damage suits from the ground above it; a storm in February 1969 washed out fifty-two feet of sewer under Douglass Street. When the Market Street Railway asked in 1938 to stop running its cars up Castro Street, the Board said no. The Castro that people come to see arrives late and in ordinary paperwork — a street closed for a fair in 1975, Supervisor Milk asking in 1978 for a fence behind the streetcar stop at Market and Castro, the street closed for an AIDS vigil in 1983, the rainbow flag at Harvey Milk Plaza made a landmark in 2024 — and running under all of it, from that same year 1975, a steady line of condominium maps.

1.name: Bernal Heights
1.summary: Bernal Heights is a hill of short steep streets, and most of the record is the work of making them: grades set and re-set on Aztec, Coso, Rutledge and Franconia, sewers dug under them, and in 1921 the first concrete pavement laid anywhere in San Francisco — a plain six-inch slab on Winfield Street. It did not always hold. Mrs. Volhart of 28 Aztec Street came down to object to a change of grade in 1939; in 1960 the owner of 37 Elsie Street told the Board the work had injured his property by sliding the embankment in the rain. Where the slope beat the roadway the city built stairs instead — up Tompkins Avenue in 1964, on the way to a school, and up Peralta Avenue in 1973 with the gas company sharing the cost. Before 1930 the hill still kept animals, fifty horses behind 3142 Mission Street and a cow at the back of 230 Prospect Avenue, and from 1916 the Board began refusing stables outright. It lit the hill a lamp at a time — one arc lamp at Ellsworth and Cortland in 1909, the whole spine of Cortland Avenue corner by named corner in 1927. The top of the hill took longer: the boulevard round the summit was ordered in 1929 and the land under it then bought a lot at a time through the 1930s, $100 and $200 a parcel, while on the south side a cut was driven through and the houses in its way sold off. Le Conte School went up on Harrison Street in 1924, and two years later its teacher in charge was given permission to rope off Norwich Street at recess. From the 1980s the city bought the slopes back for open space and began naming the trees on them — the blue elderberry at Folsom Street, the two flowering ashes outside the Bernal Heights Library, which had started life in a rented building on Cortland Avenue in 1936. Through the same years most of the new paperwork has been Mission Street and the lanes off it being split into condominiums, one final map at a time. In 2026 the Board voted a plaque into the sidewalk at 205 Mullen Avenue, where Carlos Santana was living when he was first discovered.

26.name: Pacific Heights
26.summary: Most of this neighbourhood's record is about what may stand here and what may not. The Board fixed set-back lines street by street — ten feet back on one stretch of Pacific Avenue, twenty on Green Street — and it said no a great deal: to a laundry at 2209 Pine Street in 1913, a stable at 2786 California in 1916, a sanitarium at 1902 Broderick the same year, an oil tank at 2336 Webster in 1921. When it did grant G. B. Mon a French laundry on California Street in 1925 the Mayor vetoed the permit, and a neighbour came to the hearing to speak against it. What it granted freely was fuel oil: fifteen hundred gallons under one house after another, Rudolph Spreckels at 1900 Pacific Avenue, Captain William Matson at 2225 Jackson Street. After the fire it buried water too, cisterns at Laguna and Union, Buchanan and California, Greenwich and Webster, paid off in instalments through 1909. In 1907 the Fillmore Street merchants put up fourteen electric arches over their own crossings and the city switched off eighty-two arc lights in exchange. Thirty-eight horses stood behind 2113 Pine Street in 1914. Four schools were ordered in two years around 1920, and the streets outside them were roped off at playtime — Green Street from noon to one for the pastor of St Vincent de Paul, Broderick Street whenever the Grant School children were out of the building. Two streets were closed altogether in 1932 for being too steep to drive. A hospital grew in the middle of the neighbourhood and kept asking to go underneath it — Stanford's tunnel across Clay Street in 1921, and sixty years later conduits under Clay, Webster and Sacramento for the Pacific Medical Center, which came back again in 1982 for a medical office building on Webster Street. From the 1970s the neighbourhood down-zoned itself and started naming its houses instead — the Haas-Lilienthal on Franklin Street, the Atherton on California, the Madame C. J. Walker Home for Girls and Women on Pine Street — while its flats came back to the Board one condominium map at a time, and have not stopped since.

31.name: Russian Hill
31.summary: Russian Hill was too steep to use, and the record starts with the city cutting it down. In 1916 the grade of Larkin Street between Chestnut and Francisco was reduced from 29 per cent to 16, at the property owners' own request; Francisco Street above it was reported "practically inaccessible", and the only way up, Hyde Street between Chestnut and Bay, was a 20.5 per cent slope under a worn-out pebblestone pavement that waited until 1931 to be rebuilt. The crooked block of Lombard Street was reconstructed in 1994, and by 2019 the Board was writing rules to ration the cars on it. Children raced coaster carts down Leavenworth Street in 1972 and Vallejo Street in 1974, with the Board's written permission. Polk Street along the foot of the hill was given 49 electroliers and 17 electric standards in 1913, and has been closed for its own art fair most summers since the 1970s. Above it the lanes were tidied up one by one — Hastings Place became Hastings Terrace in 1915, a street lamp went up on Macondray in 1919 and in 1948 the Board changed its name from Lane to Street. Until about 1931 it also voted on the fuel oil under each house, fifteen hundred gallons at a time. In 1966 an owner at the bottom of the hill asked to be moved from a forty-foot height limit to two hundred, and was refused. Since the 1970s most of what happens here is a building being cut into flats that sell separately, and the parking measured to the foot between named driveways — but the Board has stopped along the way to name things: the Diego Rivera fresco inside 800 Chestnut Street, a plaque for Tina Modotti outside her family's house on Taylor Street, the Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples on Larkin Street.

9.name: Hayes Valley
9.summary: Hayes Valley is where the city kept its horses. In one decade the Board licensed 125 of them at 416-418 Fulton Street, ninety-four behind 1820 Market Street, sixty-eight at 1215 Fell Street, fifty at 525 Gough — and five ponies at 915 Fulton. Then the same addresses came back as garages: 1213-1215 Fell Street was the Divisadero Street Stables in 1914 and a public garage the year after. Before any of that, in the spring of 1906, the Board's attention was called to Camp Forrest, a relief station on Laguna Street between Hayes and Fell, and to the way rations were being handed out there. The far end of Hayes Street was too steep for a plain roadway and got retaining walls, steps and railings in 1915, with a lamp at each stairway. City Hall was ordered built at the neighbourhood's eastern edge in 1913 and the High School of Commerce enlarged on Fell Street in 1922, and through those same years the Board moved Fell, Gough and Page Streets out of the residential zone and into the commercial one, block by block, while licensing the fuel-oil tank under each building — a dairy at 231 Franklin Street, a laundry on Fulton. From 2001 the record turns almost entirely to Octavia Boulevard: parking rules written to take effect once it was "completed and open for traffic", a new green handed to the Recreation and Park Department in 2005, supportive housing built on a leftover Central Freeway parcel on Fulton Street in 2008, and a plan drawn for the square mile around its junction with Market Street. Between those, steadily since the 1990s, the flats have been cut into condominiums and each new bar and shop on Hayes Street has come to the Board for its licence.

32.name: Seacliff
32.summary: Sea Cliff arrived as somebody's subdivision and was handed over to the city piece by piece: a bond posted in 1916 against the unpaid taxes on Subdivision No. 2, deeds to its streets accepted in 1923, a map approved in 1926 extending Lake Street out to Camino del Mar and opening Sea View Terrace. The sewer down California Street was paid for in 1906, before most of the houses existed, and the avenues between California and Lake were curbed and paved one at a time after that, with an arc lamp at the corner. Once the houses arrived the commonest record by far became a fuel-oil tank going in under one of them — fifteen hundred gallons at 2975 Lake Street, fifteen hundred at 2801, two hundred and fifty at the corner of Twenty-seventh and California. What the Board mostly did besides that was decide how far back from the street a house had to stand — five feet along one length of Twenty-seventh Avenue and ten along the next, ten on Thirty-second, where Joseph Novitsky filed an objection — and which of the two residential zones each corner belonged in. The Bergerot School went up on Twenty-fifth Avenue in 1908 for $37,000, and sixteen years later the Board of Education asked to rope off Twenty-fourth Avenue behind it during the recess hour. Underneath runs the sewer that carries the whole district: by 1939 a control gate at Twenty-fourth Avenue and Lake Street was holding the Richmond's flow to eighteen million gallons a day. In 1932 Villamar Avenue was renamed Twenty-fifth Avenue North, and four years later its front doors were renumbered to match. After that the record thins to almost nothing — a condominium map now and then, an argument in 2020 over a house on Seacliff Avenue, and in 2022 the naming of the old City Cemetery that lies under Lincoln Park.

37.name: Twin Peaks
37.summary: Up here the city has spent a century un-making streets about as often as making them. It closed parts of Grand View Avenue in 1930, Stanyan Street and Mountain Spring Avenue in 1931, Acme Alley the same year, a length of Portola Drive that had been the Old Ocean House Road in 1949, portions of six more streets in 1951, Raccoon Drive in 2014 — and in 2025 it gave notice that it means to vacate parts of Christmas Tree Point Road and Twin Peaks Boulevard for a promenade. What did get built had to be blasted out: permission to explode blasts to run a sewer through rock on Romain Street in 1909, on Seward Street in 1916, at Romain and Corbett in 1927. In the 1950s the sewers arrived ahead of the houses — Clarendon Avenue was sewered before it was widened, to serve the Forest Knolls and Midtown Terrace subdivisions, and the water was pushed over the hill by a pump station near Olympia Way that the city reported in 2002 had outlived itself. In 1990 the Planning Commission turned down a use proposed for 445 Burnett Avenue and the Board granted it anyway, with conditions. The names keep moving as well: Falcon Avenue became part of Market Street in 1918, and in 2023 a stretch of Palo Alto Avenue became La Avanzada Street.

19.name: Mission Bay
19.summary: For its first eighty years this was a rail yard and a tidal channel, and the record is mostly track. The Board handed out spur tracks one at a time — to the Monadnock Brick Company on Sixteenth Street in 1907, to the Pacific Oil and Lead Works off King Street the same year, to the Felton Company on Second Street in 1909, to Crane Company on Second Street in 1926 — and in 1926 it printed a list of every spur track permit granted since 1916. It bridged the Channel at Third Street with a bascule bridge in 1930, $320,000 out of a bond fund, the State Harbor Commissioners paying half. It had already put a temporary sewage pumping station on Fourth Street near Berry in 1907, and in 1912 it bought the incinerator — the Sanitary Reduction Works — for $400,000. It made the railroad pay for the street as well: in 1919 it directed the Southern Pacific to grade, curb and pave Townsend Street between Fourth and Eighth, and the company agreed to begin by April of the following year. In 1959 a printing firm was allowed to park on the Berry Street sidewalk. Then the whole place was replanned. A ground lease for a ballpark was signed in 1997 and a redevelopment plan for Mission Bay South adopted in 1998; in 2000 the Board asked that the south side of King Street be renamed 24 Willie Mays Plaza. What followed was a neighbourhood assembled out of paperwork: parts of Fourth Street vacated, the old easements under Hubbell Street given up, parks dedicated and named one by one, and condominium buildings of 99, 111, 224, 263 and 329 units approved between 2006 and 2012 with housing bonds behind many of them. Two survivors from before got their names written down — the Dunham, Carrigan & Hayden Building at 2 Henry Adams Street in 2018, and the Takahashi Trading Company at 200 Rhode Island Street in 2022.

30.name: Presidio Heights
30.summary: A good deal of this neighbourhood was cemetery first. The Board took a deed from the Laurel Hill Cemetery Association for street purposes in 1926, and when Calvary Cemetery was given up it recorded that the abandonment "has opened a new area for sub-division"; Geary Boulevard was widened past the Anzavista tract in 1947, and in 1935 St. Rose's Avenue became Anza Street. The streets were then widened out of their own frontages — fourteen feet given up along Parker Avenue in 1927, eleven feet three inches taken off the west side of Presidio Avenue by 1947 — and the Board spent the interwar years fixing how far back a house had to stand, six feet then eight then ten along Parker Avenue. The same few corners kept coming back asking to move from the residential zone into the commercial one, Arguello at California, Bush at Presidio, California at Parker, and the Board and the Planning Commission disagreed about them for a decade. Under the houses went fuel oil, fifteen hundred gallons at a time. Since 2019 nearly the whole record has been a single block: 3333 California Street, on the old cemetery land, where the Board worked through a development agreement, a conditional use, a special use district, an encroachment permit across five streets, a map for 675 flats, and in 2025 a financing district to pay for the infrastructure. Smaller arguments run underneath: a foreign-language programme for children on Sacramento Street was appealed to the Board in 2008, and the environmental report for 3333 California was conditionally reversed in 2019. At 800 Presidio Avenue it made room for fifty affordable flats beside the Booker T. Washington Community Service Center. And it has written down three names: Theodore Roosevelt Middle School in 2019, the manzanita at 115 Parker Street in 2008, and Avery Street, renamed Boswell Way that same year for the Reverend Hamilton T. Boswell.

10.name: Inner Richmond
10.summary: This grid was lettered before it was numbered, and the record catches it changing its name: "B" street became Balboa and "C" street Cabrillo, Point Lobos Avenue became Geary, California Street South became Cornwall, and First Avenue became Arguello Boulevard. The Board spent twenty years accepting the roadways block by block, then started taking the width back off the pavements — Clement Street's roadway was widened four feet in 1926 by narrowing its sidewalks. Horses were kept here in quantity: forty behind 2934 Fulton Street in 1914, and a hundred and fifty at 701 Seventh Avenue in 1923. In 1914 the Board ordered the Geary Street, Park and Ocean Railroad to pull its cable tracks out of Fifth Avenue, calling them a public nuisance. In 1928 the Frank McCoppin School was allowed to rope off Seventh Avenue twice a day, half an hour at a time, on all school days. Under the houses went fuel oil, fifteen hundred gallons at a time, until about 1931. From 1983 the argument was about Clement Street itself: the Board barred new restaurants, fast-food places and bars between Arguello and Funston for a year, then barred banks there as well, then kept extending both. Since then the street has come back to the Board one licence at a time. Off it, the flats behind have been cut into condominiums ever since the late 1970s and the kerbs measured out foot by foot for permits and motorcycles. And in 2017 it decided, conditionally, not to rescind the tax sale of the common ground of Presidio Terrace, the private street inside the neighbourhood.

15.name: Lone Mountain/USF
15.summary: The first thing in the record here is from December 1906: the United Refugees asking leave to put cottages on the unbuilt parts of Grove Street between Masonic and Clayton. Lowell High School came next — a site chosen in 1909, the land bought that year, the building ordered in 1910 for the block bounded by Grove, Hayes, Ashbury and Masonic. North of it lay the Odd Fellows Cemetery, and once that was gone the streets went in over the ground: Anza Street was cut through to St. Rose's Avenue in 1935 for $40,000, St. Rose's itself was renamed Anza the same year, and Rossi Avenue, Almaden Court, Loraine Court and a row of terraces were taken in as public streets in the years after. Stanyan Street was extended north to Turk in 1931; the following year twenty-five feet of it was closed again and deeded to two women who had paid $3,000 for the ground. Between times the ordinary business went on — forty horses at 506 Stanyan Street in 1914, arc lamps put up a corner at a time, fuel-oil tanks under the flats until about 1931 — and in 1909 Mrs. C. Nichols was given the floor to speak against a police station and stables on Stanyan Street. From the 1980s the Board was mostly being asked to let one building become something else — a private school at 350 Masonic Avenue argued over through 1985 and 1986, a twenty-person care home at 212-214 Ashbury Street in 1993, after which it urged the Planning Commission to set up a neighbourhood committee to watch the conditions. Through all of it the university has been the constant: steam and electric lines run under Parker Avenue for it in 1986, the south side of Anza Street rebuilt for its Lone Mountain campus in 1997, and Loyola Village's flats mapped in 2001.

23.name: Oceanview/Merced/Ingleside
23.summary: For its first thirty years this district was a set of avenue names being graded into existence — Plymouth, Capitol, Orizaba, Miramar, Faxon, Harold, Lee, Jules — with contractors given ninety days at a time, and some of them losing the work when they ran over. An arc lamp went up at Orizaba and Sagamore in 1908. In 1909 the president of the Ocean View Improvement Club was licensed to blast rock out of the ground at Thrift Street and Lakeview Avenue. In 1916 the Board asked that a pool of water at Farallones Street and San Jose Avenue be filled in, two boys having drowned in it. In 1921 it asked for a playground beside the Sheridan School and for a park opposite the railway station. At the end of the twenties Alemany Boulevard was cut through in lettered sections, and a house at 102 Bright Street was sold off out of its way. Then the record thins for decades and comes back along Ocean Avenue: a twenty-nine-lot subdivision at 1 Capitol Avenue in 2013, a landmark in 2016 for the Ingleside Presbyterian Church and its Great Cloud of Witnesses at 1345 Ocean Avenue, and then — three times in six months of 2024 — an ordinance requiring that the new branch library for Oceanview, Merced Heights, Ingleside and Lakeview be built on the city's own ground at 100 Orizaba Avenue.

25.name: Outer Richmond
25.summary: Owen McHugh spent years failing to finish Fulton Street. The Board gave him ninety days in July 1906, ninety more in December, ninety more the following July; then he took the next stretch, from Thirty-seventh to Forty-seventh Avenue, and needed four extensions for that as well. Around him the avenues were sewered and paved a block at a time out to the ocean, and by 1921 the western half of the Great Highway was finished, a roadway a hundred and fifty feet wide. Out at that end were things that were nowhere else in the city: thirty ostriches licensed in 1912 in the block between Forty-sixth and Forty-seventh avenues, two goats kept behind 418 Twentieth Avenue in 1914, and a sewage pumping station buried at Forty-eighth Avenue and Fulton Street — the end of a sewer system the Board had been ordering up the avenues since 1909. In 1909 the City Attorney was told to eject trespassers from Twenty-third Avenue between Lake Street and Lobos Creek. The modern record is licence after licence along Geary Boulevard and Clement Street, condominium maps on the blocks behind them, and a few things finally written down: the Alexandria Theater on Geary named a landmark in 2023, an encroachment settled the same year for the Seal Rock Inn out on Point Lobos Avenue, and a standing agreement to hang the city's emergency radio on the veterans' hospital at 4150 Clement Street.

39.name: West of Twin Peaks
39.summary: Almost everything out here arrived as a named subdivision, and the record is the city taking the names in. In 1917 the streets of Westwood Park — Valdez Avenue, Westwood Drive, Wildwood Way, Kenwood Way — were declared open public streets straight off the developer's map, and St. Francis Wood, West Portal Park and Forest Hill came the same way. St. Francis Circle was opened in 1918 out of a piece of land a hundred and fifty-five feet across where five roads met, and Junipero Serra Boulevard was paved from Ocean Avenue to the county line for fifty thousand dollars. Twice in ten days in March 1910 the San Francisco Motor Club was allowed to race cars up Nineteenth Avenue from Sloat Boulevard to the top of the hill. Between the tracts the Board spent thirty years re-setting grades on Flood, Staples, Hearst and Mangels avenues and arguing with contractors about who would finish. The tracts are still being cut finer — a single-family lot on Congo Street proposed for four in 2020, two of them undersized. The ground still moves: a landslide between Casitas Avenue and Miraloma Drive in January 2016 left the city settling claims worth up to five million dollars. Lately it has mostly been naming what is already standing — the Cowell House on San Marcos Avenue in 2015, the El Rey Theater on Ocean Avenue in 2017, the Westwood Park entrance pillars in 2023, the Gregangelo Museum on San Leandro Way in 2024 — while doing the whole thing over again at the Balboa Reservoir, sold to a developer in 2020 and given four new street names in 2023: Diego Lane, Loquat Lane, Meyer Lane and Wisteria Lane.

34.name: Sunset/Parkside
34.summary: This district was built on sand, and in December 1914 the city measured how much: test holes bored across it found bedrock 343 feet down between Santiago and Taraval, 348 feet between Fulton and Cabrillo, 398 feet between Wawona and Yorba. The first streets were redwood curbs and broken rock; the sewers in the lower Sunset had to be buried under fill to hold them up; and in 1923 the Board set aside $900 simply to shift a sand drift off Irving Street. Around that work were sixty horses in a corral between Twentieth and Twenty-first avenues, a well being drilled, and the Great Highway paved a half-width at a time. The avenues then came in one crossing at a time for forty years, with the same contractors asking for another ninety days. Schools followed the houses — the Jefferson School ordered at Nineteenth Avenue and Irving Street in 1920, an annex to the Parkside School in 1925, additions to Francis Scott Key — and in 1931 the Board ordered lighting standards the whole way along Sloat Boulevard, from Nineteenth Avenue to the ocean beach. Lately the Board has been naming what stands out here — the Trocadero Clubhouse in Stern Grove in 2021, the Mother's Building at the Zoo in 2022, the Parkside Branch Library in McCoppin Square in 2023 — and buying whole buildings for affordable housing, on Irving Street and on the Great Highway. In 2023 it closed the Great Highway Extension south of Sloat Boulevard, three thousand three hundred feet of it. And in 2013 the city recorded that the seven-foot dachshund's head was back in place at Sloat Boulevard and Forty-fifth Avenue, with a street party to mark it.

5.name: Financial District/South Beach
5.summary: The blocks between Market Street and the waterfront came back from the fire with machinery inside them. Building after building appears in the record holding a permit for an engine, a boiler and an oil tank, and the permits say what the machines were for: a hat factory at 583 Market Street, a candy factory at 49 Fremont Street, brass being melted at 83 Natoma Street and at 225 Beale Street. Rail came in behind them. One firm after another was allowed to run a siding off the Southern Pacific's tracks and into its own doors — the Enterprise Brewing Company off Harrison Street in 1908, A. Schilling & Co. on Second Street in 1916, Zellerbach Paper off Front Street in 1923, the Palmolive Company on Second Street the same year — and in 1907 the Santa Fe was granted a right of way on Spear Street, from Little Main Wharf to Mission Street. The roadways were repaved with basalt blocks on concrete, and in 1908 the Board ordered the owners of the Pacific Building to stop putting a canopy out over the sidewalk until it had worked out whether they were allowed to — the first of many arguments here about the sidewalk. That same autumn it went after the tents: "under the guise and name of clairvoyants, test mediums and fortune tellers, numerous persons have erected unsightly tents on various portions of Montgomery avenue, Kearny street and Market street." Sidewalk widths were then fixed street by street in law, twenty feet along the Embarcadero, fifteen on Post Street, and at the end of the twenties the Board began dividing the kerb doorway by doorway, writing a directory of downtown as it went: 225 Bush Street, thirty-six feet, the Standard Oil Building; 155 Sansome Street, thirty-six feet, the stock exchange, two elevators; 27 Geary Street, eighteen feet, the Owl Drug Company, one elevator. In 1943 Grant Avenue between Bush Street and Broadway was renamed Mei-Ling Way for Madame Chiang Kai-shek. In 1947 the city counted more than sixteen hundred people crossing one half-hour stretch of Montgomery Street sidewalk; in 1949 it abandoned its plans to widen California Street and Post Street, and went at the car in bulk instead — a study in 1950 found a twelve-hundred-car garage would pay for itself in a single downtown block, and by 1953 the Board was weighing a plan for one of three thousand seven hundred and fifty stalls on Mission Street between Third and Fourth. After that the ground went the other way: Powell Street closed to cars in 1972, tables and chairs licensed in Maiden Lane at lunchtime from 1973 — a permit still being amended in 2025 — while the towers went up behind hoardings the Board granted one street at a time, Sacramento Street for the Levi Strauss building, Front Street for the Embarcadero Center's walkways. In 1982 it started writing the old buildings down instead: the Phelan and the Flatiron on Market Street, the Kohl Building on Montgomery the year after. On the South Beach side the same ground was replanned and sold as flats — the Rincon Point and South Beach plan widened in 1992, sixty-two units at 401 Main Street in 1994 — and lately the Board has kept at the Transbay blocks, taken progress reports on retrofitting 301 Mission Street, and gone back to naming: the Allegory of California mural at 155 Sansome Street in 2021, One Montgomery Street, the old Crocker bank, in 2022. In between it decides, week by week, who may sell a drink and where: a wine bar in the Mira on Folsom Street, a lounge at 88 Kearny Street, a shop at 221 Sansome Street.

33.name: South of Market
33.summary: South of Market is where the city has always put the work. The first permits after the fire are for engines and boilers in workshops — two of them at 553 Brannan Street for a planing mill — and for stables: forty horses for Jones & McGill off Folsom Street in 1907, twenty-two for the New French Baking Company on Tehama Street in 1913, twelve for Blumenau & Neuman on Natoma Street in 1914. The Board did not just say yes. In March 1916 it refused R. O'Banion a stable at 1237 Folsom Street, took the application up again in May, and granted him a stable "for 12 horses only" — he had asked for thirty. Four years earlier a neighbour, Mrs. Hannah Banker, had come and stood before the Board to argue against a stable on Stillman Street. Laundries were licensed the same careful way, with the power written into the permit: hand or electric only for Paul Verdier at 310 Seventh Street in 1908, an engine and boiler for the Galland Mercantile Laundry on Eighth Street, eight horsepower for a rescue mission's laundry at 884 Folsom Street, and a five-thousand-gallon oil tank behind the Bay City Steam Laundry at 910 Folsom Street. When the Board started dividing the kerb doorway by doorway around 1930, the names it wrote down here were makers and warehouses, not banks: forty-five feet at 485 Brannan Street for Liggett & Myers Tobacco, eighteen at 1093 Mission Street for the Chicago Artificial Limb Company, eighteen at 1464 Howard Street for the Stella Metal Casket Company. Then the city moved its own difficult business in. The building that went up in the block between Seventh, Bryant, Harrison and Harriet was given to the successor firm of the architects who designed City Hall, and in 1957 a new street was cut between Sixth and Harriet to serve the new Hall of Justice; from there the record is lease after lease — six floors and half a basement on Jessie Street, a public health clinic at 250 Fourth Street, the Public Defender's offices on Boardman Place. The workshops became flats twice over: bonds in 1985 to buy and repair the empty Hueblein Building at 601 Fourth Street, then a run of live-work conversions around 2000 — The Lofts at 712 Bryant Street, 950 Harrison Street, 1150 Folsom Street. The end of that boom is in the record too. In December 2000 the Board asked whether the space "newly vacated by the closing of Pets.com at 435 Brannan Street" might be taken for courtrooms. It still licenses the district drink by drink, down to a music venue's licence for 1535 Folsom Street in 2024, and it is still housing people here: 459 hotel rooms at 1231 Market Street kept on through 2020, sixteen and a half million dollars of bonds for the Knox residential hotel at 241 Sixth Street, a lease at 1076 Howard Street for the health department.
